theme: Jeremiah called; the two evils; broken cisterns
readingInstruction: Read Jeremiah 1:1-3:5. Jeremiah is the longest book in the Bible by word count, and it is the story of a reluctant prophet. Read his call in chapter 1, and then notice the two evils that God names in chapter 2.
settingTheScene: Jeremiah was a priest from Anathoth, a village near Jerusalem. He was called as a young man in the thirteenth year of Josiah, around 627 BC, and he prophesied for over forty years, through the reform, the fall of Jerusalem, and the flight to Egypt. His message was unpopular. He was beaten, imprisoned, and thrown into a cistern. He is called the weeping prophet, but he was also a man of great courage.
observation: “Before I formed you in the womb I knew you, and before you were born I consecrated you; I appointed you a prophet to the nations” (1:5).
“Ah, Lord GOD! Behold, I do not know how to speak, for I am only a youth” (1:6).
“Do not say, I am only a youth; for to all to whom I send you, you shall go” (1:7).
“Behold, I have put my words in your mouth” (1:9).
“For my people have committed two evils: they have forsaken me, the fountain of living waters, and hewed out cisterns for themselves, broken cisterns that can hold no water” (2:13).
“What wrong did your fathers find in me that they went far from me?” (2:5).
“My people have changed their glory for that which does not profit” (2:11).
“Have you not just now called to me, My father, you are the friend of my youth?” (3:4).
interpretation:
Jeremiah’s call is among the most intimate in Scripture. God says he knew him before he was formed. Before birth, he was set apart. The call is not an accident or a career. It is the purpose of his existence. Jeremiah objects at once: “I am only a youth.” God’s reply is typical: don’t say that. Go where I send you, speak what I command, and “be not afraid of them, for I am with you to deliver you.” God then touches his mouth. The word of the LORD is something God puts in the prophet.

His commission has two sides: “to pluck up and to break down, to destroy and to overthrow, to build and to plant.” Four verbs of judgment and two of restoration. Judgment comes first.

Chapter 2 is one of the great statements of sin in the Bible. God remembers the devotion of Israel’s youth, like a bride following him in the wilderness. Then he asks, “What wrong did your fathers find in me?” It is the question of a husband who cannot understand why his wife left. Then the two evils. First, they forsook the fountain of living waters. A spring is endless, fresh, and free. Second, they dug their own cisterns, cracked and leaking. Idolatry is both ingratitude and folly. The nations do not change their gods, and Israel has changed its glory for what does not profit.

The pattern is the human heart: to leave the source of life and then to spend all our energy on things that cannot hold what we put in them. Every generation digs cisterns. Money, approval, success, and pleasure are broken cisterns.

Yet the chapter ends with an invitation. God says, “Return.” The door is still open.
connection: Jesus said to the woman at the well, “Whoever drinks of the water that I will give him will never be thirsty again” (John 4:14), and “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink” (John 7:37). Paul says he was set apart before he was born (Galatians 1:15). Matthew 16:14 notes that some thought Jesus was Jeremiah. Ephesians 2:10 says we are God’s workmanship, created for good works.
application:
Name one “broken cistern” that you have gone to for satisfaction. Bring your thirst to Christ.

If you have felt too young, too inexperienced, or too weak for what God has asked, hear his words, “I am with you.”

Pray for a fresh sense of being known and called by God.
prayerPrompts: Confess the cisterns you have dug for yourself.
Ask him to draw you back to the fountain of living waters.
Thank him that he knew you before you were formed.
